name: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)
mechanism: Hydrophilic bile acid that reduces proportion of hydrophobic (toxic) bile acids (chenodeoxycholic, deoxycholic acid) in bile pool. Protects cholangiocytes from toxic bile acid-induced injury. Reduces cholesterol secretion into bile and absorption from gut. Immunomodulatory effects (reduces MHC class I expression on hepatocytes). Improves bile flow in cholestatic liver disease
dosing: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC): 13-15mg/kg/day PO in 2-4 divided doses (or single dose). Usually 250mg TDS or 500mg BD. Take with food. Gallstone dissolution: 8-12mg/kg/day in divided doses for months-years (rarely used - surgery preferred). Primary sclerosing cholangitis (off-license): 15-20mg/kg/day (controversial benefit). Pruritus in cholestasis: 10-15mg/kg/day
contraindications: Acute inflammation of gallbladder or bile ducts. Complete biliary obstruction (no decompression). Frequent episodes of biliary colic. Calcified (radio-opaque) gallstones (won't dissolve). Non-functioning gallbladder. Caution: severe hepatic decompensation (limited efficacy)
interactions: Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol) bind UDCA → ↓ absorption (separate by 4-6h, or avoid). Antacids (aluminium-containing) ↓ absorption. Ciclosporin: UDCA may ↑ absorption (↑ levels - monitor). Oestrogens, clofibrate ↑ cholesterol in bile (↑ gallstones - may antagonize UDCA). No significant CYP interactions
monitoring: LFTs (ALP, bilirubin, transaminases) - assess biochemical response (aim for ALP normalization or <1.5× ULN in PBC). Response at 12 months predicts long-term prognosis. Lipids (may improve). Pruritus severity. If gallstones: ultrasound at 6-12 months (assess dissolution). Signs of disease progression (jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy - indicates advanced disease). Consider liver biopsy if uncertain diagnosis or poor response
pregnancy: Limited data, but appears safe. Used in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP) - reduces pruritus, may improve fetal outcomes (controversial). Benefit likely outweighs risk in PBC if already established on treatment. Continue if needed
sideEffects: Common: diarrhoea (dose-related, usually mild - reduce dose if troublesome), nausea, abdominal pain. Uncommon: pruritus (paradoxical worsening initially in some - usually improves), rash, headache, dizziness. Rare: exacerbation of liver disease (decompensation in advanced PBC - stop if occurs). Calcification of gallstones (prevents dissolution)
pharmacokinetics: Well absorbed in small intestine (90%). First-pass metabolism in liver (conjugated to glycine/taurine). Secreted into bile, undergoes enterohepatic circulation. Bacterial deconjugation in colon, reabsorbed. Gradually enriches bile acid pool (displaces toxic bile acids). Minimal systemic exposure (acts locally in biliary system). Excreted in faeces
clinicalPearls: Brand: Ursofalk, Ursogal, Destolit. MAIN USE: primary biliary cholangitis (PBC, formerly PBC). ONLY disease-modifying therapy for PBC. Improves LFTs (especially ALP), delays progression to cirrhosis, reduces need for liver transplant, prolongs survival. Start early (non-cirrhotic stage for best outcomes). RESPONSE: assess at 12 months - 'complete response' (normalization ALP, bilirubin <1× ULN, transaminases <2× ULN) predicts excellent long-term prognosis. 'Partial response' (ALP <1.5-2× ULN) also beneficial. Non-responders (~30-40%): consider second-line (obeticholic acid, fibrates off-license, liver transplant if progressive). PRURITUS: may help in cholestatic pruritus (PBC, PSC, ICP). Not always effective - alternatives: cholestyramine (first-line for pruritus), rifampicin, naltrexone, sertraline. PSC (primary sclerosing cholangitis): controversial - no proven benefit in large trials, but some centers use off-license. Not routinely recommended. GALLSTONE DISSOLUTION: rarely used (surgery preferred). Only for small (<15mm), radiolucent (cholesterol), non-calcified stones in functioning gallbladder. Takes 6-24 months, high recurrence (50% at 5 years). ICP (intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy): reduces maternal pruritus, may improve fetal outcomes (bile acids toxic to fetus - ↑ stillbirth risk). Evidence mixed - NICE/RCOG suggest may be used. Monitor fetal wellbeing, consider early delivery. ALTERNATIVES if PBC non-responder: obeticholic acid (FXR agonist, but hepatotoxic in decompensated disease - BLACK BOX WARNING), fibrates (bezafibrate, fenofibrate - off-license, ↓ ALP, ? long-term benefit), liver transplant (advanced disease, decompensation, refractory pruritus). Well-tolerated: diarrhoea main side effect (dose-reduce if needed). LIFELONG therapy in PBC - explain importance of adherence. Monitor annually (LFTs, clinical assessment). If decompensated cirrhosis develops despite UDCA, consider transplant evaluation
indication: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) - disease-modifying therapy. Dissolution of radiolucent gallstones (rarely used). Symptomatic treatment of pruritus in cholestatic liver disease. Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (off-license)
